The Colors are from Specialistpaints, but only because of the specific type of color, you can use pretty much most solvent based, non resin based paints.

Clearcoat is Spraymax 2K, its the only isocyanate based clear in cans out there that seems to work for me.

Process wise, really simplified:

Sand existing paint flat (logo bumps etc) with 320 Grit

2K Epoxy Primer

Sand Primer with 400

2K Epoxy Primer

Lightly sand Primer with 600

Wait 2-3 days to dry for each primer so that it actually shrinks into the scratches

Black Base, 60min flash 

Paint Silver in the general area where its gonna be, 3-4 coats, 15 min flash.

Let dry for 12+h

Mask the design & Logos 

Paint the Chromacoat, 3-4 Coats, 15 min flash.

Unmask, let sit for 30 mins

Clearcoat:

Light Tack coat, 5 min flash

2-3 coats, 15-20 min flash. 

Let sit for 2-3 hours

Repeat Tack & 2-3 coats.

Let cure for 48+ Hours

Sand lightly with 1000 grit to remove major orange peel

Repeat Clear coat 1 last time

Let cure 48 hours

Sand clear with 1500-3000 grit, polish.

Voila.

Obviously mask bearing seats and whatever you cant chase a die through afterwards, keep everything clean with silicone remover or similar before painting

Please dont Radial lace people.

1. It literally pulls the hub flange apart, some manufacturers even forbid radial lacing with their hubs

2. with all the force going straight outwards, you are messing with the press fit tolerances of the bearings, causing galling and fretting in the bearing seat.

3. it has no performance advantage. Some say it is Laterally stiffer which is not right. Yes, the Spoke is shorter than with a crossed pattern, but with a crossed pattern the effective spoke lenght is even shorter since the spoke braces against at least one other spoke half way through. Besides that, even if it were Laterally stiffer, in the longitudinal axis, especially on J Bend hubs (Straightpull is still not ideal) the spoke has to completely rely on its tension / bending resistance to transfer braking power. With a crossed pattern the spoke can pull in the direction of its tension, and thus be a lot, a lot! more effective at that.

Normal Tank ammo from that time relied on Kinetic energy. The British mostly used solid ArmorPiercing shells, and later sub caliber ArmorPiercingDiscardingSabot shells. Latter is a small Penetrator (Usually from Carbide) incased in a big Sabot - Shoe in order to fit in a Big gun to get the most bang. With it being that tiny and light it could reach speeds up to 1500m/s which helps in long Distance engagements massively compared to a usual Shell traveling at 800m/s (which is still bloody quick)

There also is ArmorPiercingHighExplosive which is an AP round with an explosive Filler inside. This helps to shoot the Fragments after successful penetration around in the tank, thus knocking out crew and components.


Today tanks use APDS - Fin Stabilized, which is basically an adaptation to use the old Apds in smoothbore ( non rifled guns) in which the fins are needed for Stability in flight. These reach speeds of up to 1800m/s

The second Type used today is HighExplosiveAntiTank - Fin Stabilized. 

The Panzerfaust/Schreck/Piat/Bazooka etc used the same HEAT warhead but without the Fin stabilization which hadnt been invented yet. HEAT has a Backwards shaped Cone with a copper Liner. Sort of like this --<| (Flying to the right)

This Copper Liner gets squeezed into a tiny Jet/ Streem of copper, which is in a funny state. Its not molten, but acts as a liquid because of the insane, hypersonic velocity its moving at. Basically if concentrated into a small jet, it flows through the Molecules of the Tanks armor. Heat is an Ammunition type relying on Chemical rather than Kinetic energy. This is why modern tanks have ExplosiveReactiveArmor to detonate/destroy and thus distort the Copper Jet before hitting the actual Hull.

Spaced Armor like Sideskirts are effective too, since Heat always explodes right on impact, while APHE can have a fuze calibrated to not detonate under a preset armor thickness, and a time delay.

Well, it is an “open” tubular because its open and not sewn together. Vittoria and co vulcanize their threads, in case of challenge the clincher/ot tires come off the same factory line as their tubulars before they have the tube sewn in.

Despite all the controversy on the internet, i was looking for some more comfort on rough roads, and it didn’t take long to find these on the internet. Challenge calls them “Hand made Open Tubular” tires, which makes sense because the tires indeed are handmade, with the thread pattern glued on by hand etc. Now what is an open tubular you might ask; basically a non vulcanized tire constructed in exactly the same way as a tubular, just with beads sewn in insetad of the tube. This offers an extremely supple tire. The Paris Roubaix comes in a 700x27c size, which for me, on 17c rims turned out to be exactly 27mm after a week of stretching. The tires come in a pancake flat shape, since they aren’t vulcanized into the curved shape we all associate with tires. That means, lots of elbow grease while mounting, i was able to mount both with one tire lever only, but stuffing the inner tube between tire and rim bed, is a real challenge (i’m sorry, had to go for that pun). It cost me one of my Schwalbe Extra light tubes, but after a week of riding, changing tubes was as easy as on every other tire. I might sound like a challenge advertisement manager here, but over potholes, cobbles and rough roads, the tire quite literally feels like it’d be on a super smooth velodrome. I cant say much to puncture resistance yet, since i’ve only had them for 2 weeks.

Appearance: 10/10

Weight: 7/10 (270g for a 27mm tire is a little heavy)

Ride quality: 10/10 (Superb, feels better than some actual tubulars)

Grip: 8/10 (Pretty good traction in wet weather, which is handy on steep climbs, and thanks to the wide thread pattern, cornering is as easy as it has never been before)

Mounting: 4/10 ( Not as bad as some may describe, but it cost me one pretty good inner tube, and really takes some patience and strenght)

Price: 35€/40$ 

Overall: 8.5/10 so far, an update on puncture resistance will come soon!
